stories.headline: U.S. Employers Added Only 57,000 Jobs in June, Less Than Half of May's Total
stories.summary:
The Labor Department reported Thursday that U.S. employers added just 57,000 jobs in June, sharply below the prior month's revised figure of 129,000 and well under economists' expectations. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.2% from 4.3%, but the decline was driven largely by discouraged workers leaving the labor force rather than new employment. The report signals that businesses remain broadly cautious about the economic outlook amid elevated inflation and weakening consumer confidence.

The hospitality sector was a significant drag, with restaurants, bars, and hotels cutting 61,000 positions — a surprising result given expectations that the ongoing FIFA World Cup in U.S. host cities would generate temporary job gains. Retailers shed an additional 7,500 jobs. Offsetting gains came from healthcare, which added nearly 47,000 positions, and professional and business services, which added 36,000 jobs. Hiring figures for April and May were also revised downward substantially.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking in Portugal Wednesday, reiterated the central bank's intent to hold rates firm until inflation is clearly under control. The Fed's benchmark rate sits at approximately 3.6%. Economists note that the weak jobs number, combined with three-year-high inflation and post-pandemic lows in consumer confidence, points to an economy in a prolonged "low-hire, low-fire" equilibrium where existing workers have some security but job-seekers face long searches.

The report complicates the outlook heading into the second half of 2026. The economy expanded at a 2.1% annual rate in the first quarter, but forecasters increasingly expect a slowdown in the April-June quarter. The divergence between upper-income households — which continue to spend — and middle- and lower-income households pulling back is sharpening, with the restaurant industry citing this "K-shaped" pattern as a key driver of job cuts.

stories.headline: Update: McConnell Suffered Apparent Cardiac Arrest at Home Before Hospitalization, EMS Dispatch Audio Reveals
stories.summary:
Audio from an emergency medical services dispatch call dated June 14 reveals that paramedics were sent to Sen. Mitch McConnell's Washington, D.C., home in response to a report of an unconscious person who appeared to have suffered a "cardiac arrest." The 84-year-old Republican senator from Kentucky was subsequently hospitalized, and his condition and timeline for returning to the Senate remain publicly unknown. The new detail is materially more serious than earlier reports, which described only that McConnell had been found unconscious.

McConnell, the longest-serving Senate party leader in U.S. history, has faced multiple health episodes in recent years, including a series of freeze episodes in 2023 during which he appeared to lose awareness mid-sentence at public events. He announced his retirement from the Senate leadership position in 2024 but remained in his seat. His absence has not been formally acknowledged by Senate leadership, and his office has provided minimal public comment.

The disclosure raises fresh questions about Senate continuity and the health transparency standards applied to senior lawmakers. McConnell's seat and potential incapacity could carry procedural significance depending on the legislative calendar and any close votes. No timeline for his return or public health update has been provided by his office or Senate Republican leadership.

stories.headline: Sen. Tillis Declares Trump's SAVE America Act 'Dead,' Citing Midterm Timing
stories.summary:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) declared Wednesday that the SAVE America Act — President Trump's stated top legislative priority — is effectively "dead" in the Senate because there is insufficient time to enact new federal election rules before the 2026 midterm elections. Tillis said that even if Republicans could secure the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster, which he indicated is unlikely, the implementation window has closed. The bill, which would establish a proof-of-citizenship requirement to register to vote in federal elections, has been a central demand of Trump and many House Republicans.

The announcement marks a significant setback for a White House that has treated election integrity legislation as a cornerstone of its second-term agenda. Supporters of the bill argue that proof-of-citizenship requirements are necessary to ensure only eligible citizens cast ballots in federal races. Opponents, including all Senate Democrats and some voting rights advocates, contend the requirement is redundant — non-citizens are already barred from voting — and would disenfranchise millions of eligible voters who lack ready access to documentary proof of citizenship.

Tillis's public break with the White House on this issue is notable given his past alignment with Republican leadership. His statement signals that Senate procedural realities and the midterm calendar have effectively rendered the bill moot for this election cycle, even as the House passed a version of the measure earlier this year.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Financial Disclosure Shows $2.2 Billion in 2025 Earnings, Over $1 Billion from Cryptocurrency
stories.summary:
President Trump's mandatory financial disclosure report, made public this week, shows he earned at least $2.2 billion in 2025 — his first year back in office — a sum presidential historians describe as unprecedented and far exceeding any previous president's White House-era earnings. Trump reported $1.4 billion from cryptocurrency alone, including $635 million in royalties from Celebration Coins, the entity linked to his $TRUMP meme coin launched just before his second term began, and more than $500 million from World Liberty Financial, a crypto firm co-founded by his sons and associates of his Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff.

The disclosure has reignited debate over presidential conflicts of interest. Critics, including Democratic lawmakers and government ethics advocates, argue the figures illustrate an unprecedented blurring of official policymaking and private financial gain, given that the Trump administration has simultaneously shaped federal cryptocurrency regulation. The White House rejected those characterizations, with deputy press secretary Anna Kelly stating that "neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest" and that all actions are taken "in the best interest of the American people."

Trump's 2025 earnings were nearly four times his reported 2024 income of $622 million. Historians note that past presidents from both parties took extensive steps to separate their finances from their official duties, citing examples ranging from Harry Truman's modest Army pension to George W. Bush's blind trust. Supporters of Trump argue his business success predates and is independent of his presidency, and that financial disclosure laws are functioning as intended by making the information public.

stories.headline: Dangerous Heat Dome Engulfs U.S. Northeast Ahead of Fourth of July, Temperatures Could Top 100°F
stories.summary:
Multiday extreme heat warnings were issued Wednesday for New York, Boston, Philadelphia and surrounding areas as a heat dome — a high-pressure system that traps heat and humidity — pushed east across the U.S. just days before the nation's 250th anniversary celebrations. The National Weather Service forecast temperatures in the high 90s Fahrenheit for the Northeast, with Philadelphia and Boston potentially reaching 100°F or higher by Thursday; humidity will push the heat index even higher.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged residents to seek air-conditioned spaces and warned that triple-digit heat over multiple days poses serious risks, particularly for those unacclimatized to such conditions. In Orange County, New York, air conditioning failed on a bus carrying Junior ROTC cadets, resulting in multiple heat-related illnesses and hospitalizations. Medical experts warned that the combination of high temperatures and humidity can cause heat exhaustion and heat stroke at lower thresholds than in drier climates.

The heat wave arrives as millions of Americans are expected to gather outdoors for Fourth of July parades, concerts, and public events across the region, raising public health concerns. Organizers of major events in Boston — including the traditional public reading of the Declaration of Independence — are monitoring conditions. The heat dome has already been affecting the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic states over recent days.

stories.headline: Update: Vatican Excommunicates Society of St. Pius X Bishops and Priests, Declares Group in Schism
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV formally declared the traditionalist Society of St. Pius X in schism Thursday and excommunicated its bishops and priests after the group consecrated four new bishops without papal authorization. The Vatican emphasized that only the pope may approve bishop consecrations, which maintain the apostolic succession linking the Church to Jesus's original disciples; unauthorized consecrations sever that connection and constitute a fundamental break with Rome.

The Society of St. Pius X was founded in 1970 by Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre in rejection of the Second Vatican Council's reforms. Its bishops were previously excommunicated in 1988 after Lefebvre performed unauthorized consecrations; those excommunications were lifted by Pope Benedict XVI in 2009 as part of an effort at reconciliation. Thursday's declaration marks a definitive rupture, with the Vatican stating the group has placed itself outside full communion with the Catholic Church.

The move affects tens of millions of traditional Catholics worldwide who have attended SSPX chapels and received sacraments from its priests. The excommunications raise immediate pastoral questions about the validity of marriages, confessions and other sacraments administered by SSPX clergy going forward. The Vatican's action underscores Pope Leo XIV's resolve to enforce doctrinal discipline even at the cost of further fracturing a conservative wing of the global Church.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran Peace Talks Continue in Qatar as Hormuz Tensions Persist
stories.summary:
U.S. and Iranian negotiators met separately Wednesday with Qatari and Pakistani mediators in Doha, with Qatar announcing "positive progress" and agreement to continue discussions. The next round of talks will be scheduled after the funeral of Iran's former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, set for Saturday in Tehran. U.S. Mideast envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner represented Washington; Iran's top negotiator Kazem Gharibabadi attended on Tehran's side.

The talks aim to convert an initial ceasefire and interim Strait of Hormuz agreement, reached Monday, into a permanent settlement ending the war that began February 28 when the U.S. and Israel struck Iran. Key sticking points include Iran's insistence on controlling shipping routes through the strait and levying passage fees — a position the U.S. and Gulf Arab states firmly reject — as well as the status of Hezbollah in Lebanon.

The stakes are enormous for global energy markets. A fifth of the world's oil and natural gas transited the strait in peacetime, and markets have swung sharply since the war began. Oil prices have been declining on signs that Hormuz traffic is gradually resuming, though a foreign container ship ran aground Wednesday on an Iran-unapproved route, which Tehran used to reassert its claimed authority over the waterway.

This is a material update on the previously covered U.S.-Iran Doha talks: negotiators met in person Wednesday, Qatar confirmed progress, and a timetable tied to Khamenei's funeral has been set for the next session — new concrete developments since the last report.

stories.headline: Boy, 11, Crashes Truck Into Monks on Pilgrimage in Thailand, Killing Eight
stories.summary:
An 11-year-old boy lost control of a pickup truck he had taken without his parents' permission and crashed into a column of 35 Buddhist monks walking in single file on a road in northeastern Thailand on Thursday, killing eight and hospitalizing 14 others, four of them critically. Five monks died at the scene in Mukdahan province, roughly 600 kilometers northeast of Bangkok; three more died at hospital. The group had set out on a 260-kilometer pilgrimage walk just 30 minutes before the crash.

Security camera footage shared by a local rescue organization shows the monks proceeding in a line along the road's edge before the truck swerves and plows into them at full speed. Police said the vehicle was taken without permission and that the cause of the accident remains under investigation, though witnesses reported the truck appeared to be swerving before impact. The boy is in custody and will be questioned when child protection officers arrive.

Buddhist monks hold a revered place in Thai society, and public processions are common throughout the country. Thailand has one of the world's worst road safety records, with speeding, drunk driving and weak enforcement cited as chronic problems. The provincial governor said the incident "should be a lesson not just for our province, but for the public in general."

stories.headline: Gaza Patients Dying While Waiting for Medical Evacuations Approved Under Ceasefire
stories.summary:
At least 300 Palestinians have died waiting for medical evacuations from Gaza since a U.S.-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Hamas began last October, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry and figures used by the World Health Organization. An estimated 15,000 patients currently await treatment abroad, including people with war injuries and conditions such as cancer, and at the current pace of transfers — 1,977 people evacuated since the ceasefire — the backlog could take years to clear.

The process requires patients to pass security clearances from Israel, any transit countries, and the receiving nation, and to be accepted by a host country willing to treat their specific condition. The BBC documented the case of Amina Abu al-Kas, who received medical board approval to leave Gaza for treatment of an aggressive necrotising infection that had spread to her skull. Her son said she died on May 29 still waiting for clearance; two weeks after her death, the hospital called to say her paperwork had been approved.

The WHO's representative for the occupied Palestinian territory told the BBC that recipient countries are often highly selective about the patients they will accept, adding complexity to an already bureaucratic process. The situation highlights ongoing humanitarian conditions in Gaza despite the ceasefire framework, with medical access remaining sharply constrained more than eight months after the truce began.
